extracted.intended_audience: educators, instructional designers, administrators, and researchers in online/distance education
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for designing, developing, delivering, and supporting high-quality online/distance learning courses, including infrastructure, technology, pedagogy, assessment, and student support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of emerging modalities and engagement features
rubrics_metrics.description: Online learning has to include mobile learning, e-gaming, online communities, and learning management systems that engage each user.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book argues online learning for the next generation must incorporate mobile and game-based approaches, community/social features, and LMS tools designed to engage individual learners rather than relying on a single mode of delivery. Examples: mobile 'in-your-pocket' learning, social software suites (e.g., Me2U).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design grounded in proven learning theories
rubrics_metrics.description: The development of effective online learning materials should be based on proven and sound learning theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors emphasize behaviourist, cognitivist, constructivist (and emergent connectivist) contributions—select strategies according to what is being taught (facts vs. processes vs. real-life application). Instructional design choices must reflect theoretical bases rather than technology fashions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learner-and-learning-focused design
rubrics_metrics.description: Online learning involves more than presentation; 'the learner and the learning process should be the focus of online learning.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Materials must be designed with learners' needs, contexts, and learning processes central. Avoid treating technology as an end: technology should enable pedagogically-sound interactions and support, not replace them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional strategy over medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructional strategy, not the technology, is what influences the quality of learning; to promote higher-order thinking, online learning must create challenging activities that enable learners to link new information to old, acquire meaningful knowledge, and use metacognitive abilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks that foster reflection, meaningful knowledge construction, and transfer. Beware the anti-pattern of assuming switching media alone (e.g., moving content online) produces learning gains without redesigning activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: High authenticity, interactivity, and collaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Online learning should have high authenticity (students learn in the context of the workplace), high interactivity, and high collaboration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor realistic, situated tasks and interactive/collaborative activities. Use simulations, workplace projects, and team assignments to increase authenticity. Low-authenticity, passive content is discouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of learning objects for flexibility and reuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning objects will be used to promote flexibility and the reuse of online materials; online learning materials should be created so that they can be redesigned for different learners and different contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure materials modularly to allow repurposing and adaptation for diverse learners and settings. Encourage versioning and local adaptation as part of open educational practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide adequate and continual learner support
rubrics_metrics.description: Online learning must be done right: materials must be designed properly, with the learners and learning in focus, and adequate support must be provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support includes tutoring, technical help, library/e-resources, and administrative services. Supports should be flexible, clear, and continually available; lack of support undermines learner success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infrastructure planning and organizational readiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Developing an infrastructure for online learning requires planning, structural and organizational attention, system components and interfaces, and considerations such as human resources, decision-making, and training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should design infrastructures that can evolve amid rapid change; lacking structural, cultural, or financial prerequisites increases risk. Evaluate interfaces among components and invest in staff training and governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select technologies that support learners' needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Technologies and features should be chosen for their capacity to aid learners (not solely to help instructors); consider blogs, wikis, social software and other tools that have become prominent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess technological affordances against pedagogical goals. Avoid adopting tech because it is fashionable; prefer tools that explicitly enable targeted interactions, authentic tasks, or assessment strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match media attributes to pedagogical models
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider attributes of media and the modes of presentation and learning performance they support in relation to influential learning models; choices of delivery/presentation medium have pedagogical implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse what each medium can support (e.g., synchronous vs asynchronous, text vs multimedia) and select to align with desired learning outcomes. Recognize trade-offs and avoid one-size-fits-all media adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan for evolutionary/ongoing technological change
rubrics_metrics.description: Any designed online learning infrastructure must be able to evolve and work in a context of constant and accelerating change to accommodate changing student needs, technologies, and curricula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design systems and policies that support upgrades, interoperability, and iterative redesign. Build capacity for continual review and improvement of tools and content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of instructional media developers and MIDE (quality control)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructional media developers and the Multimedia Instructional Design Editor (MIDE) bring pedagogical standards to course development and carry out quality control functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include media specialists and MIDE-like roles on course teams early to facilitate communication among authors, learners, and technical staff; use their expertise to enforce pedagogical standards and quality assurance, especially for multimedia and aggregated learning objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial analysis and cost-aware decision making
rubrics_metrics.description: Making relevant financial decisions about technology requires detailed understanding of fixed, variable, recurring, and other costs to understand cost and revenue implications of online learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform cost analyses before adopting technologies; consider total cost of ownership, development, maintenance, and support; use financial insights to make sustainable choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality assurance is relative and contextual
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality in online education is a relative experience realized largely through individual expectations; quality assurance contexts and competing paradigms must be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine jurisdictional quality standards (examples provided for Australia, UK, Canada, US) and adapt QA frameworks to institutional goals and student expectations. Use formative and summative measures and be explicit about quality criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and design for interaction types (six forms of interaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Online learning involves six forms of interaction and these are critical for engaging and supporting learners and teachers; models consider collaborative and independent study modes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map course activities to interaction types (learner–content, learner–instructor, learner–learner, etc. as described in the text) to ensure balanced engagement. Choose design patterns appropriate for collaborative or independent modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt constructivist/connectivist approaches where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a shift toward constructive learning (learners construct their own meaning) and the introduction of connectivism to exploit connections to knowledge and people afforded by the Internet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design opportunities for learners to create meaning, network, and leverage connections (social networks, resources). Use activities that foster knowledge construction, critical reflection, and networked learning practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching presence model: cognitive, social, teaching presence
rubrics_metrics.description: Creation of an effective online educational community involves three critical components: cognitive presence, social presence, and teaching presence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design instructor roles, facilitation strategies, and activities to ensure all three presences are cultivated. Use facilitation, prompting, feedback, and community-building to maximize teaching effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Library and information support tailored to e-learners
rubrics_metrics.description: Library support for e-learners should provide e-resources, e-services, and consider human factors; virtual libraries and collaborative practices are important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure remote access to resources, user-centered services, and integration of librarians into course support. Design library services with attention to communication and human usability factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student-support best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Student supports should be flexible, clear, and continually available, aiming to develop learner independence while ensuring supports are readily available when needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide multiple support channels (call centres, help desks, online FAQs, tutoring), clear guidance on processes, and consistent availability. Monitor and refine support based on learner feedback and retention data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize prior learning (PLAR) and use portfolios
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior Learning Assessment and Recognition (PLAR) should be situated in online learning; portfolios composed by learners and assessed by faculty allow recognition of knowledge acquired inside and outside formal education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design PLAR processes to balance credential quality control with valuing learners' time. Provide clear portfolio requirements, rubrics, and faculty assessment procedures to award appropriate credits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use open-access and sharing to improve reach and quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Open-access licensing (e.g., Creative Commons) and sharing course content as open educational resources increases access and allows materials to be refined, versioned, and adapted by academics around the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider open licensing to expand reach, encourage adaptation, and foster community improvement of materials. Anticipate issues of attribution, version control, and institutional service offerings that support open-content strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design online team projects with explicit teaming processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective online team projects require explicit attention to team chartering, trust-building, leadership, communication technology, diversity awareness, monitoring progress, and contingency planning for technology failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish a team charter early, set expectations, create mechanisms to build trust (competence, commitment, character), choose robust communication tools, monitor contributions, manage workload, and plan for technical issues. Leadership should foster culture conducive to rapid trust development.
